claims.text: Severe plastic deformation can be applied through thermomechanical processes such as additive friction stir deposition.
Severe plastic deformation by AFSD induces dynamic recrystallization in high-entropy alloys.
AFSD-induced dynamic recrystallization refines a high-entropy alloy to a nanocrystalline or near-nanocrystalline grain structure.
As-cast high-entropy alloys can have mixed FCC/BCC or related multiphase microstructures.
The baseline as-cast high-entropy alloy has a coarse grain structure.
The mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys depend in part on phase constitution, with BCC phases generally associated with higher strength and FCC phases with higher ductility.
Grain refinement increases the density of grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries impede dislocation movement in high-entropy alloys.
The resulting inhibition of dislocation motion increases hardness, yield strength, and ultimate strength according to a Hall–Petch-type relationship.
AFSD-processed high-entropy alloy will have significantly higher hardness than the as-cast baseline.
AFSD-processed high-entropy alloy will have significantly higher yield and ultimate strength than the as-cast baseline.
Reductions in average grain size will correlate with increases in hardness and strength.
The comparison will hold composition and processing environment constant while comparing as-cast and AFSD-processed states.
The proposed behavior is limited to processing conditions that cause substantial dynamic recrystallization without additional phase formation.
Excessive thermal exposure can cause grain growth or phase decomposition and thereby limit the proposed strengthening behavior.
Other mechanisms, such as precipitation hardening, may contribute significantly in some high-entropy alloy systems.
A lack of statistically significant grain refinement or a lack of correlation between grain size and improved properties would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
